q: A friend says Firebase means "no backend work at all". What is the best reply?
o: You still write and test security rules
Only true on the paid plan
why: Google runs the servers, but your security rules decide who can read and write your data. That part is your job.

q: In the Notes app, a user saves a note. What does Firebase check before Firestore saves it?
o: The ID token, then security rules
why: Firebase first checks who the user is (ID token), then whether the rules allow the write.

q: Which product would you use to send a reminder to a user's phone?
why: Cloud Messaging delivers push notifications, usually sent from a Cloud Function or server.

q: Your app must send a push to all users when an admin clicks a button. Where should the sending code run?
o: In a Cloud Function or server
why: Trusted actions must run in a place users cannot copy or change, such as a Cloud Function.

q: A team needs reports that join ten tables with complex filters. What is the honest advice?
o: Firebase may be a poor fit here
why: Firestore cannot join collections in one query. Heavy relational reporting is a reason to consider other tools.

q: What is a good way to keep lock-in costs low with Firebase?
o: Keep Firebase calls in a few files
Copy the config into every file
why: If Firebase calls live in a few places, moving to another provider later means rewriting less code.

q: Because Firebase is built on Google Cloud, every Firebase project is also a Google Cloud project.
why: Fact. This is why you can add other Google Cloud services to the same project later.

q: With Firebase you pay per server, so a bug that reads data in a loop costs nothing extra.
why: Myth. You pay per read, write, storage and download, so a read loop can raise the bill quickly.
